query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Tribocorrosion in HEAs is governed by a dynamic interplay between mechanical wear‐induced removal and oxidation‐driven self-healing of a protective passivation layer.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy with a homogeneous, single-phase structure (for example, Fe20Co20Ni20Mn20Cu20) deposited via microwave cladding on SS-304.
generation.intervention: Subject the HEA to cyclic sliding wear in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 60 °C, with intermittent pauses that permit oxidation.
generation.conditions: Tribological sliding under moderate load in an aqueous chloride environment at 60 °C, where liquid conditions and oxygen remain available to support oxidation kinetics.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formed oxide layers (such as chromium oxide or high-entropy spinel phases) that periodically regenerate during rest phases.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical sliding removes portions of the pre-existing oxide film, but during pauses in loading the reactive alloy elements rapidly oxidize and regenerate a protective layer. The net degradation rate is then determined by the balance between wear-induced film removal and oxidation-driven film reformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline sample in which oxidation is deliberately inhibited (thus preventing effective film regeneration), the sample with an actively regenerating oxide will exhibit lower combined degradation (reduced wear and corrosion rates).
generation.baseline: An identical HEA sample modified (via chemical surface treatment or alloying) to inhibit oxidation and thereby block the self-healing mechanism.
generation.boundary: This mechanism holds under conditions where the temperature and oxygen content are sufficient to drive oxidation (e.g., 60 °C in an oxygenated aqueous environment) but may fail in low-oxygen or overly aggressive chemical conditions that prevent oxide formation.
generation.uncertainty: Although moderate temperature tribocorrosion studies (e.g., PMC10908794 and PMC10456374) support enhanced durability with self-healing, the precise kinetics of oxide regeneration under cyclic wear remain to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with an unimpeded oxidation process and another where oxide formation is chemically inhibited. Subject both to identical cyclic sliding wear tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution at 60 °C. Monitor the evolution of the oxide film using XPS or TEM, measure wear track volume via profilometry, and assess corrosion rates using potentiodynamic polarization.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the sample with inhibited oxide formation does not exhibit significantly higher overall degradation (increased wear and corrosion) compared to the freely oxidizing sample, the hypothesis that dynamic film regeneration governs tribocorrosion will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

The Fe, Co, Ni, Mn, and Cu are combined to produce the coating, which is employed as a protective layer on the surface of SS-304 steel. These alloying components can enhance corrosion-resistance and serve as sacrificial anodes to shield the underlying SS-304 steel by being present in the coating. When subjected to corrosive conditions (3.5 wt. % NaCl media) the initial corrosion processes commence. The development of dark-spots on the surface of SS-304 is conceivably caused by chloride-ions that can penetrate the coating and commence localized corrosion reactions. These dark areas could be indications of localized corrosion, such as pitting or crevice corrosion, where the protective oxide layer on the SS-304 may have been compromised or where the coating may have been breached. The corrosion processes can be considerably accelerated by the high temperature exposure (800 °C). It may encourage the diffusion of corrosive species into the SS-304 substrate and through the coating. Increased corrosion rates and improved chemical reactions may result from this.
